title: Lawyer gets probation in Chicago for helping hide fraud by disgraced LA celebrity attorney Tom Girardi

Tom Girardi’s high-flying legal career may have been made for Hollywood, from a portrayal in the film “Erin Brockovich” to a tumultuous marriage to reality TV star Erika Jayne, but its stunning collapse started in a federal courtroom in Chicago nearly six years ago.

Known for going after big companies whose negligence caused tragic consequences, Girardi’s famed Los Angeles firm, Girardi Keese, was suing Chicago-based Boeing on behalf of families of victims from the 2018 Lion Air crash in Indonesia that killed all 189 people aboard. The firm had collected millions in settlement payments from Boeing that it was supposed to disburse to clients beginning in March 2020.

Instead, the case took a dramatic turn before U.S. District Judge Thomas Durkin, who found that Girardi had been stealing the funds and covering it up. The revelations sparked a nationwide investigation into misconduct by Girardi and others at his firm, ultimately landing Girardi in prison for nearly 7 ½ years.

On Thursday, a final chapter in the story of Girardi’s downfall unfolded down the hall from Durkin’s courtroom, where Keith Griffin, a former lawyer for Girardi Keese, was sentenced to two years of probation for criminal contempt for helping hide Girardi’s lies about why the victims had not been paid.

During the 90-minute hearing, U.S. District Judge LaShonda Hunt said she found it “disappointing and reprehensible” that Griffin and other lawyers who worked for the firm used the trust placed in them to lie to vulnerable victims and attempt to deceive the court.

“Part of the reason why this went on is because of the status of these victims, who didn’t know what to do,” Hunt said. “I don’t think you can separate out the fact that there were innocent victims here who trusted the lawyers that they hired and those lawyers intentionally did not protect their rights. They had no other recourse.”

While Hunt said Griffin played “ostrich” by sticking his head in the sand, he was ultimately the least culpable player in the scheme, who was “left holding the bag when it all imploded.” In rejecting the prosecution’s call for a three-month jail sentence, the judge also said Griffin’s bad choice to try to cover for his famous boss does not negate an otherwise “upstanding” career spent advocating for often-desperate clients.

“One day, this too will pass, and hopefully you will have lessons to share with your children and grandchildren and others to show that you have bounced back from a horrible period in your life,” Hunt told Griffin, seated at the defense table in a charcoal suit and dark blue tie. “You are not your worst moment.”

Before the sentence was handed down, Griffin stood at the lectern and let out a sigh before apologizing to the Lion Air clients and their families, as well as to Durkin and the justice system as a whole. He said he’s often thought of the lectures he’d give his children about standing up to bullies and doing the right thing, even when it’s difficult.

“I am embarrassed and ashamed because I did something that is particularly difficult for me to accept,” he said. “I was a hypocrite … When it was my turn to speak truth to power, I was weak, and that is something that I will live with for the rest of my life.”

Girardi was once among the most prominent lawyers in the nation, often representing victims of major disasters against powerful companies. One lawsuit against California’s Pacific Gas and Electric utility led to a $333 million settlement and was portrayed in the 2000 Julia Roberts film “Erin Brockovich.”

Girardi’s fame hit another level when he married “The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills” star Erika Jayne — a former cocktail waitress 33 years his junior — and appeared on the show himself dozens of times between 2015 and 2020.

The misconduct in the Lion Air case first began to come to light in 2020 when Chicago firm Edelson PC, which served as local counsel for the plaintiffs, discovered Girardi’s firm had failed to distribute millions in payments made by Boeing beginning that March.

Court records uncovered during hearings before Durkin show that over the course of about six months Girardi instructed Griffin and others in his firm, including his son-in-law, David Lira, to give a variety of excuses to the clients about the failure to pay them the settlement money, including blaming complications from the COVID-19 pandemic and nonexistent tax issues.

In November 2020, an increasingly anxious Griffin sent a note to his boss warning him that Edelson was about to take action in court, saying he had “12 days to pay the Boeing clients the balance of their funds,” which at the time amounted to about $3.2 million, records show.

“If they do not receive their funds by Nov. 30th, they have indicated that they are all filing bar complaints and a criminal complaint with the DA’s office,” Griffin wrote. “This could not be more serious.”

On Dec. 3, 2020, Edelson indeed filed a rule to show cause that prompted Durkin to freeze Girardi’s assets and hold him in civil contempt in an attempt to recover the lost funds. At a hearing later that month, Durkin also warned Jayne to stop selling items with ties to her husband, including designer clothing from a firm where he had a stake.

“Apparently these are clothes she is selling that belong to her. I don’t know whether assets she is selling are considered community property (but) if she’s selling assets that are property of Thomas Girardi, either whole or in part, you need to inform her of the danger that puts her in,” Durkin told an attorney for the reality star at the time.

Jayne was never accused of any wrongdoing in the case.

But three years after the allegations in the Boeing settlement emerged, Girardi was indicted in separate cases filed in Chicago and Los Angeles on charges he stole more than $18 million from clients around the world, including a California couple whose son was paralyzed in a car crash, an Arizona widow whose husband died in a boat accident, and a dozen families who lost loved ones in the Lion Air crash in the Java Sea.

Though he had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease, a judge found Girardi competent to stand trial and he was convicted by a jury of wire fraud in 2024 in Los Angeles, where U.S. Attorney Martin Estrada called him a “Robin-Hood-in-reverse.”

Now 87, Girardi was sentenced last year to seven years and three months in prison and ordered to pay a $35,000 fine and $2.3 million in restitution to former clients. He’s serving his time at a medical prison facility in Rochester, Minnesota, and is not due to be released until 2031, records show.

Prosecutors in Chicago later moved to dismiss the indictment here due to Girardi’s age and lengthy prison sentence. But cases against Griffin, Lira and Christopher Kamon, longtime Girardi Keese chief financial officer, moved forward, with all pleading guilty to their roles in helping cover wrongdoing at the firm.

In court Thursday, Griffin’s attorney, Mark Werksman, sought to portray his client’s missteps as “a process crime” against the court, saying he was just a salaried employee and that it was the “larger than life” Girardi, who jetted around the world with his reality star wife while feeding “phoney-baloney” excuses to Griffin to relay to clients.

When Griffin tried to get his boss to make good on the settlement money, Girardi would say something about it being “above your pay grade,” Werksman said.

“He’s given the unenviable task of passing along Mr. Girardi’s BS to Edelson, and he didn’t know it was BS,” Werksman said. “Mr. Griffin didn’t know until it was too late that he couldn’t trust his boss, the only boss he’d ever had.”

In asking for jail time, Assistant U.S. Attorney Jared Hasten acknowledged that Girardi was the “villain” in the case, but said his fraud would not have been possible with enablers like Griffin who were willing to look the other way.

Hasten also said that no matter how difficult it might have been to rat on his boss, Griffin owed it to his clients to call the judge and tell him what was going on.

“He does not tell the world what he knows internally, which is that Tom Girardi is a thief,” Hasten said. “This is terrible, terrible conduct, and if there is a case where a lawyer should go to jail for a couple months, based on these facts I think it’s this one.”

The Associated Press contributed to this report
